source.title: TaxoSAE: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders through Taxonomic Logic
source.authors: Xin-Yu Guo; Minglai Yang; Clayton T. Morrison; Eduardo Blanco; Mihai Surdeanu

page_placements.theme: SAE and dictionary feature properties: interpretability scores, purity and stability vary by domain, layer and dictionary design (not neurons)

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study discusses SAE features as units for concept readout and control, but it does not test whether neuron poles have one main job, evaluate neuron explanations on held-out activations, or test the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures concentration of taxonomic activations across SAE slots. These are supervised or selected SAE features, not neuron poles or the neuron-explanation tests named in the claim versions. The reported concentration results are recorded as related findings, not as tests of a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes TaxoSAE, a supervised stacked sparse autoencoder that binds taxonomic concepts to designated SAE slots in fine-tuned GPT-2 small and Qwen2.5-0.5B. It reports readout, steering, selectivity and SAE-slot concentration. It never measures how many of the models' own neurons or neuron poles have one main job. It does not score neuron explanations on held-out text and does not examine InceptionV1 or neuron-level attribution graphs. Its concentration metrics (EffFeat, Top1C) describe supervised SAE slots built for concentration, not neurons arising in training. It mentions only in passing, citing prior work, that unsupervised SAE features split concepts. It therefore bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that TaxoSAE (stacked SAEs plus a taxonomic alignment loss) gives more accurate taxonomy readout and more precise control than the baselines on two factual QA taxonomies. They add that it reads unseen concepts at their hypernyms and that extending it to larger models is future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and evaluates a taxonomically structured SAE; it does not reproduce the neuron-pole audit or neuron-explanation methods in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The layer used affects results: layer-wise sweeps show layer-dependent readout and steering, and Qwen2.5-0.5B control changes with layer. The paper notes that the selected Qwen layer was not tuned.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised TaxoSAE slots carry each non-terminal concept on about one unit (EffFeat 1.0–1.7; Top1C 89–100%). Unsupervised SAE features selected by difference-in-means spread each concept over about 130–415 effective features, with Top1C of 1.3–7.5%. This holds on GPT-2 small (Bio and Animal) and on Qwen2.5-0.5B (Bio).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small fine-tuned LMs, SAE slots supervised to match a taxonomy concentrate concept activation far more than the best-matching unsupervised SAE feature.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper includes a GitHub reference but no URL in the text provided.
record.problems: The experiments use two small, three-level taxonomies and fine-tuned models; the authors report English-only evaluation and state that larger models remain future work. The Qwen experiment uses a single seed, and the paper notes that its chosen layer was not tuned. These limitations also mean the SAE-slot concentration results do not establish neuron-pole job shares.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result directly measures neuron poles or tests neuron explanations on held-out activations, so no results are assigned to V1–V7. Other readout, steering, ablation, and selectivity outcomes are omitted because they do not measure the claimed neuron-pole job share or the listed explanation tests.

untested.parts: All of it: no audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles.
All of it: no neuron-level interpretability shares in any model.
All of it: no InceptionV1 or polysemantic-neuron analysis.
All of it: no measure of interpretable-neuron share against architecture or tools.
All of it: no attribution graphs built from neurons.
All of it: no explanations written from activating examples and tested on firing.
All of it: no simulation-based explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T6/discusses classification is correct. The study evaluates SAE features and never analyses raw neurons. The rows are mostly the study's own method compared with its baselines, which is appropriate only under fits_no_version. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The share of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one or two jobs, and the share not understood.
Shares of interpretable neuron poles across models, architectures, and scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and recursive generalization.
Architecture, regularization, tools, and the proposed change in interpretable-neuron share.
Attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons and their reconstruction error.
Whether explanations written from activating examples predict firing on new activations.
Automated simulation-based scores for neuron explanations on new text.

relation.reason: It neither tests nor uses the claim. The text never discusses neuron interpretability, but discusses is the closest label available for a topically related SAE paper.

tranche.reason: Proposes and evaluates its own supervised SAE (TaxoSAE). It measures SAE-slot concentration, readout and control, with no neuron-level audit or neuron explanations.

source_check.notes: All rows measure how concentrated concepts are in SAE slots or features (TaxoSAE vs unsupervised SAEs), not in the models' own neurons, so they are rightly unlinked. GPT-2 rows omit layer (6 Bio, 9 Animal). Unsupervised EffFeat/Top1C are the same for Random and DiffMean (App. J). Qwen results come from a single seed at an untuned layer 12.

statements.correction: TaxoSAE non-terminal (L2/L3) EffFeat 1.0-1.7, Top1C 89.0-100.0% (GPT-2 small on Bio and Animal, Table 1; Qwen2.5-0.5B on Bio, Table 4). Unsupervised SAE dictionaries: non-terminal EffFeat 132.5-415.6, Top1C 1.3-7.5%. Both metrics are computed without post-hoc feature selection and are identical for Random and DiffMean (§6.1; App. J). These are SAE slots or features, not model neurons.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but it says the fragmentation comes from features selected by difference-in-means. The paper computes EffFeat/Top1C on all SAE activations without post-hoc selection, and the values are identical for Random and DiffMean.
